content: The annual incidence of delusional disorders is estimated to be between 0.7 and 3.0 cases per 100,000 individuals. The annual prevalence of delusional disorders is estimated to be between 24 and 30 cases per 100,000 individuals. Delusional disorder accounts for approximately 1-2% of all admissions to inpatient mental health facilities. The incidence of first-time hospital admissions for delusional disorder is estimated to be between 0.001% and 0.003%. The lifetime morbid risk of developing delusional disorder is estimated to range from 0.05% to 0.1%. According to the DSM-5, the estimated lifetime prevalence of delusional disorder is 0.2%. This is significantly lower than the lifetime prevalence of other major psychotic disorders, such as schizophrenia (0.3% to 0.87%) and bipolar I disorder (0.24% to 0.6%). In studies of patients receiving mental health treatment, the prevalence of delusional disorder has been reported to range from 0.5% to 1.2%. The true prevalence of delusional disorder is likely underestimated because most individuals with the condition do not recognize it as an illness and therefore do not seek treatment. Delusional disorders are relatively uncommon in psychiatric practice. However, this may also be an underestimation, as individuals with the disorder often lack insight into their condition and avoid psychiatric evaluation. The annual incidence of delusional disorders is approximately 0.7 to 3.0 cases per 100,000 individuals. The annual prevalence of delusional disorders is approximately 24 to 30 cases per 100,000 individuals. Females are more frequently affected by delusional disorder than males. Delusional disorder typically affects individuals in middle to late adulthood. The age range for first-time hospital admissions for delusional disorder is generally between 33 and 55 years.
